NSS-77TR RECORD

⸻

NSS-77TR — Monthly Core Summary [2026-05]

May functioned as a transition-closure / NSD-6 re-entry month, not a simple continuation month. Total logged days reached 31, with 27 completed sessions and 4 Rest / Delay entries. The month included multiple previous-stage graduations, full NSD-6 line replacement, new lower-level technical entries, and the first practical STATUS → RECORD transfer test. The main character of May was therefore not just training continuation, but system conversion: completed 7-level lines became the base for new movement maps.

May should be defined as

previous 7-level closure + NSD-6 line transition + new movement mapping + record-system integration.

Overall character of the month

May began by closing several lines from the previous transition block. Adv. PL PU, HSPU, BAPL45, A. OAP, and Str. FL Row all reached closure or graduation-quality markers. After those closures, the system did not continue by simply adding more volume to the same movements. Instead, it shifted into new entries: PHSPU, Str. PL PU, OAP Negative, FL Row, BAPL60, Str. 360 Pull, and Negative + A. Pistol.

The important point is that these new entries began at lower levels without behaving like regressions. The earlier 7-level base carried over as support tolerance, rhythm familiarity, lever control, and signal clarity. May therefore acted as a conversion month where old endpoints became new baselines.

Current working hypothesis

Lower-level re-entry after 7-level closure is not a reset. In the current system, it functions as a mapping phase for longer levers, deeper ROM, new setup constraints, and more specific signal interpretation. Progression quality should be judged by how quickly the new line attaches cleanly, not by whether the visible level number is high.

Rest / Delay entries also remained compatible with the rotation. They did not break the system as long as the next actual completed session resumed from the correct line state.

Primary stage-transition lines

HSPU / PHSPU

HSPU completed 7.7 E2 and can be marked as graduated. The key May change was not a single peak set, but repeated operating stability under non-ideal starting condition. Several sets reproduced 6+ continuity, and one important in-set recovery appeared when a forward-diagonal bent line was held, re-centered, and continued without coming down.

After graduation, the vertical push line transitioned into PHSPU. PHSPU immediately changed the problem from free-balance / floor support into deeper ROM and parallette setup management. Wrist load reduced clearly, while entry / exit cost and face-to-hand ROM became the main practical variables.

Adv. PL PU / Str. PL PU

Adv. PL PU completed 7.7 E2 and graduated cleanly. The 7-level horizontal push no longer behaved like a major event. It felt more like an operating checkpoint, with local shoulder load fading into the background and trunk control remaining the main task.

After that, the line transitioned into Str. PL PU. The new working shape was not yet a clean full straddle line. It appeared as a compact frog / straddle-L-like intermediate push. The main limiter shifted from pressing output to pelvis, hip, and leg-position mapping.

A. OAP / OAP Negative

A. OAP closed at 7.7 E3. It remained one of the hardest lines, but May showed the clearest improvement in output and stamina since A.OAP became the vertical-pull line. Dead-hang pass-through became more available, sway stayed low, and S1 reached the best output so far.

The line then moved into OAP Negative. This confirmed that full one-arm negative is not yet available. The current negative work remains support-dependent, with close-hand start, main-arm loading, hook-like grip tendency, forearm demand, and one-arm dead-hang transition becoming the main information points. OAP Negative now functions as a cleaner range / load-mapping phase rather than a volume target.

Str. FL Row / FL Row

Str. FL Row completed 7.7 E2 and closed the previous horizontal-pull transition block. The endpoint was not a polished full straddle row, but stable frog-like working row plus Str reference access. Row identity remained intact even when late-session ROM reduced.

FL Row then entered better than expected. Removing the straddle split reduced pelvis / hip noise, and the working shape became closer to a bent-knee full-lever-like row. The row trajectory was small but alive. This suggests that the row pattern transferred successfully from Str. FL Row into a cleaner full-line preparation.

BAPL45 / BAPL60

BAPL45 completed 7.7 E2 and graduated through pendulum-based continuous rotation. The important carryover was rhythm, not static strength. Lever fixation, toe extension, and rebound rotation became repeatable under 7-level volume.

BAPL60 then entered as the new Complex Push line. The first exposures corrected the assumption that 80–90° BAPL would be almost impossible. BAPL60 worked through rebound-assisted / pendulum-driven rotation rather than static holding. By 5.5 E1, the line attached cleanly: S1 showed mild entry signal, S2 connected the pendulum rhythm, S3 stabilized lever / rotation synchronization, and S4 reached near-90° rotation through inertia rather than forced output.

Adv. 360 Pull / Str. 360 Pull

Adv. 360 Pull had already graduated at the end of April, and May converted that rhythm base into Str. 360 Pull. The new line immediately exposed setup limits: doorway space, back-lever-side foot contact, limited straddle width, and near-full-like lever moments.

Str. 360 Pull progressed through 3.3, 3.5, and 5.5 exposure. The movement became more familiar, but forearm accumulation and back-side pelvis opening remained the main costs. The next task is smoother pass-through rhythm and cleaner back-lever-side pelvis extension, not static hold polishing.

Conditioning / Lower-chain line

The lower-chain line shifted from Pistol Negative volume toward assisted-ascent mapping. Pistol Negative progressed through 6-level and 7-level exposure, but May clarified that more negative volume was no longer the highest-value target. R side remained landing-control dominant, while L side showed clearer bottom-hold access and early ascent-initiation signal.

Negative + A. Pistol entered after this. Ring-assisted ascent was rejected because it changed the ascent trajectory. Floor-hand-assisted ascent became the current transition method. L side connected better through bottom hold into light hand assist, while R side still needs mapping around hand position, forward body curl, foot pressure, and assisted-ascent path.

Burpee 40×3 stayed in the conditioning slot, but its role became more diagnostic. Palm / wrist support-contact warning appeared earlier in the month, then disappeared after pistol arms-forward adjustment. Later sessions showed R shoulder pop during jump-back transition, with farther-forward hand placement reducing the pop. Conditioning therefore continued as both circulation work and support-contact signal inspection.

Signal / fatigue status

May showed good structural tolerance despite repeated line transitions. Shoulder signals appeared frequently, but most were residual, rhythm-related, setup-related, or post-set traces rather than stop-level warnings. R shoulder residual remained the most common repeated trace, especially around band work, support lines, BAPL rotation, and burpee transitions.

Palm / wrist support-contact warning appeared but did not become a persistent limiter. PHSPU reduced wrist burden through parallettes, while OAP Negative and Str. 360 Pull shifted load toward forearm, grip, and hook-control demand.

Lower-chain signals stayed mostly non-painful. Knee pops appeared around pistol bottom work, but the more important limiter was bottom-hold control, ankle / foot-pressure mapping, and assisted-ascent path. DOMS or ordinary local fatigue did not define the month. Movement quality and signal interpretation mattered more than soreness.

System interpretation

May confirmed that NSD-6 is now functioning as a rotation of transition lines rather than a list of isolated exercises. Earlier main movements are becoming warm-up exposures, signal checks, or base conditions for the next line.

HSPU became the base for PHSPU. Adv. PL PU became the base for Str. PL PU. A. OAP became the base for OAP Negative. Str. FL Row became the base for FL Row. BAPL45 became the base for BAPL60. Adv. 360 Pull became the base for Str. 360 Pull. Pistol Negative became the base for Negative + A. Pistol.

This is the clearest system-level change in May. The month did not simply add more difficulty. It reorganized completed lines into a new operating map.

Monthly conclusion

May was a transition-closure and NSD-6 re-entry month. The month closed several 7-level lines, then converted them into new lower-level technical entries. These lower-level entries did not behave like regressions. They carried over the previous block’s support tolerance, rhythm base, lever awareness, and signal clarity.

Overall, May should be marked as

the month where the previous 7-level transition block closed, NSD-6 became the active operating structure, and new movement lines began mapping from a stronger base rather than from zero.

The next phase should not rush level escalation. The main task is to preserve clean mapping, rhythm attachment, and signal stability while each new line builds its own usable operating pattern.

NSS-77TR — Monthly Core Summary [2026-04]
April functioned as a
7-level re-entry / expansion month
, not a simple continuation month.
Total sessions reached
27
, marking one of the highest monthly frequencies so far. The month included multiple 7-level entries, one clear graduation, full-bottom pistol access, HSPU continuous-volume PR, and alate-month neural downshift signal. The main character of April was therefore not just high volume, but
high-frequency operation under expanding level zones
.
April should be defined as:
7-level expansion + first current-stage graduation + full-ROM lower-chain unlock + high-frequency neural-limit observation.
Overall character of the month
April was a high-density month where the system operated close to its current upper frequency range.
Unlike March, which involved a visible downshift / interruption window during stage transition, April showed mostly continuous execution through the majority of the month. The system did not collapse underincreased level demand. Instead, most main lines either entered 7-level, stabilized 6-level, or opened new ROM territory.
However, the late-month forced shutdown / neural fatigue event suggests that the limiting factor is likely not local muscular fatigue or joint irritation, but
cumulative neural execution load
under high-frequencyoperation.
Current working hypothesis:
~15 consecutive sessions
may represent a high-adaptation / high-focus zone.
~18–20 consecutive sessions
may become a neural downshift risk zone.
Downshift signs are not typical DOMS or structural fatigue, but repeated sleepiness, mood drop, driving drowsiness, and automatic sleep / shutdown.
This should remain a working hypothesis, not a fixed rule yet.
Primary stage-transition lines
HSPU
HSPU made one of the clearest jumps in April.
Earlier HSPU work still depended heavily on kick-up quality, first descent attachment, and shallow-ROM continuity. By 4/26, HSPU entered
7.7 E1
, and the session produced a new continuous-volume PR with
7continuous shallow-ROM reps
. Several later sets reproduced 7-rep continuity or strong segmented completion, confirming that the first set was not a one-off event.
The main gain was still
continuity and work capacity
, not ROM depth.
Key changes:
7 continuous shallow-ROM reps became available.
Wrist local burden reduced clearly.
Support load spread through palm / lower forearm / wrist line.
Kick-up / line attachment remained the primary limiter, not pressing strength.
HSPU moved from fragmented execution toward repeatable volume operation.
Compared with the previous 6.6 E2 pattern, April’s 7.7 E1 was a different level of continuity and total work capacity.
Str. FL Row
Str. FL Row stabilized through
6.6 E2
.
The key April change was not full horizontal straddle row completion, but the emergence of a clearer
near-horizontal reference hold
and a more stable compact working row.
Early reference holds approached horizontal with only slight pelvic fold. Lower-lat / side-lat tension became strongly perceptible during the initial reference hold. Under accumulation, the actual working form stilleconomized toward a frog-like / compact advanced-straddle intermediate shape, but row identity stayed intact.
Most important improvement versus E1:
No clear progressive ROM / trajectory collapse appeared.
Side-lat / lower-lat pumping confirmed the pulling line stayed active.
Reference hold became a marker, not the main task.
Working form remained repeatable under accumulation.
This line now functions as a
Str lever preparation line
, and its later graduation should naturally transition toward Full FL Row rather than over-polishing straddle form as an endpoint.
Adv. 360 Pull
Adv. 360 Pull became the first clear graduation of the current stage set.
On 4/28,
Adv. 360 Pull 7.7 E2
completed successfully and can be marked as
graduated
. The major transition was mechanical, not merely volumetric.
E1 showed that slower or hesitant rotation increased forearm burden and strap instability. E2 reproduced the faster rhythm solution from the beginning of the session.
Key changes:
Faster rhythm reduced front-back strap swing.
Forearm was no longer the main limiter.
Front / back lever transition points were passed through rather than held with static braking.
Inertia shifted from a load source into a usable rhythm component.
S5–S6 still showed remaining output.
S7 closed without breakdown.
Adv. 360 Pull changed from a
forearm / strap-control task
into a
rhythm-driven rotation task
.
Next progression can move toward
Str. 360 Pull
, with space management, ring length, and lever-length handling expected to become the next practical issues.
Complex Push / BAPL
BAPL45 moved into
7.7 E1
and showed a major rhythm / lever-fixation shift.
The key change was the transition from stop-reset control into pendulum-style continuous rotation. The session produced a peak set where lever fixation, rhythm, rotation, and energy reuse integrated clearly.
Key points:
Rotation timing and lever fixation improved through the session.
Continuous pendulum-style rotation became available.
Mid-session rhythm reduced rep-time and improved efficiency.
Peak work suggested perceived ROM beyond a pure 45° class.
Later sets showed fatigue and reduced ROM, but structure remained intact.
This line now appears to be transitioning from “finding the rotation” to “operating the rotation.”
Conditioning / Lower-chain line
April contained the clearest lower-chain event so far:
full-bottom pistol access opened
.
On 4/21, both sides entered true full-bottom pistol depth for the first time. This did not feel like gradual ROM extension, but more like a previously locked lower range suddenly opening.
Then:
4/25:
Pistol Negative 3.5
4/30:
Pistol Negative 5.5 E1
The 3.5 session established repeated full-bottom entry and early bottom control. The 5.5 session expanded full-ROM negative volume from
15 total reps to 25 total reps
.
Current phase:
range opened → range repeatedly entered → bottom control begins
Key observations:
R side can enter full bottom and achieved brief holds, but bottom posture retention remains inconsistent.
L side shows better descent stability and bottom control.
Knee pops appear mostly around first deep-bottom entries, without pain.
Bottom-hold limitation likely involves ankle / foot-pressure control and opposite-leg active hold, not just strength.
Slow glute landing is useful bottom-braking practice, not a failed rep.
Burpee remained strong overall. 4/25 produced
4:17
with light perceived effort, near PB range, but 4/30 was intentionally cut early due to L palm / upper-limb support signal rather than systemic fatigue.
Conditioning therefore served two roles in April:
1.
Lower-chain ROM expansion and consolidation.
2.
System cleanup / circulation between high-level push-pull-complex blocks.
Signal / fatigue status
April showed strong structural tolerance.
DOMS and same-day condition became less decisive for session outcome. Even with mild residuals, most sessions could proceed because load was absorbed through structure rather than concentrated locally.
Major positive signal trends:
Local wrist burden decreased during HSPU.
Shoulder signals were mostly residual or post-set, not movement-limiting.
Lat / lower-lat activation became clearer in pull lines.
BAPL and 360 Pull shifted toward rhythm-based load distribution.
Pistol full-bottom work produced pops without pain and no major residual restriction.
However, late April also produced a neural downshift / forced rest signal. This differed from ordinary fatigue:
repeated sleepiness during the day
driving drowsiness
mood drop / nervous system flatness
automatic sleep after work
no clear local muscular or joint failure
This suggests the likely limiter is
cumulative neural execution load
, especially around 18–20 consecutive high-focus sessions.
System interpretation
April confirmed that NSD-6 is functioning as a six-directional synergy system rather than a simple list of exercises.
The six main session types:
vertical push
horizontal push
vertical pull
horizontal pull
complex push
complex pull
appear to raise the shared base of scapular control, ribcage / pelvic stacking, grip / forearm support, lever handling, and rotation rhythm.
The important point is not that one movement directly causes another. The synergy is broader:
each movement type raises the base conditions that make the next movement less foreign.
Examples:
Str. FL Row prepared the Str lever before Str. 360 Pull.
Adv. 360 Pull graduated the rotation rhythm before Str. 360 Pull.
HSPU warm-up exposure contributed to main-session HSPU continuity.
L Pull-up continued shifting from former output work toward warm-up / signal-check status.
Full-bottom pistol access began converting the lower-chain line from range limitation into bottom-control work.
Past main tasks are gradually becoming future warm-up positions or signal checks. This remains one of the clearest signs of system maturation.
Monthly conclusion
April was a high-frequency expansion month.
The month did not merely accumulate sessions. It changed several baselines:
HSPU moved into 7.7 with new continuous-volume PR.
Adv. 360 Pull graduated at 7.7.
Str. FL Row stabilized at 6.6 with better trajectory retention.
Pistol opened full-bottom depth and moved into negative-volume consolidation.
Conditioning remained strong, though late-month upper-limb support signal required early cut.
A neural downshift limit near 18–20 consecutive sessions became more plausible.
Overall, April should be marked as:
the month where 7-level operation became real across multiple lines, the first current-stage graduation occurred, and the system’s high-frequency neural limit began to show its outline.
The next phase should not rush volume upward.
The main task is to carry April’s expanded level baselines into May while watching whether high-frequency neural downshift repeats under similar conditions.

NSS-77TR — Monthly Core Summary [2026-03]
March should be defined as a 3-level stage-transition month that had already begun around lateFebruary to early March, not as a month of fresh 7-level entry.
No new 7-level zone entry occurred during March. Pistol 7.7 remained a conditioning-fixed line withinNSD-6 and should be treated separately from stage-transition evaluation. The actual significance of themonth was that the system had already entered a stage-transition process from the 3-level zone, thenpassed through a visible neural downshift / interruption window, and later re-stabilized with clearerruntime continuity by month end. Total session count still reached 23, so despite the interruptionphase, overall monthly volume was not low.
Overall character of the month
March was not a smooth build-up month. It was a transition month with interruption inside it. Early-to-mid March included downshift-related breaks, but the month as a whole still maintained meaningfuldensity. The key point was not uninterrupted accumulation, but whether the stage-transition linesreconnected under runtime conditions after the downshift period. By month end, multiple linesshowed exactly that.
Primary stage-transition lines
HSPU
HSPU remained the only line operating under explicit hold / repeat treatment rather than normalforward progression. Early 5.5 E2 was still dominated by instability, shallow ROM, fragmentation, andearly termination under pressure-type head signal. However, 5.5 E3 became the first session sinceentering the 3-level HSPU phase that felt meaningfully satisfactory: shallow-ROM continuity becameusable, 5 continuous reps were reproduced multiple times, body-line fixation improved, and shoulderload was essentially absent during main work. The main gain was continuity, not ROM depth. Warm-upHSPU exposure appears to have contributed directly to this change.
A.OAP
A.OAP showed one of the clearest transition improvements in March. By 5.5 E2, the earlier R/L gapnarrowed significantly. The L side caught up and even became the more stable side, while the R sideremained stronger early but less stable / less durable later. Top-range ROM was pursued withoutopposite-shoulder contact or trunk-rotation compensation. Post-session load concentrated in the innerbiceps bilaterally rather than the shoulders. This line no longer looked like an uncertain entry attempt,but like a line beginning to organize itself under actual runtime rules.
Adv. PL PU / BAPL complex push lines
These lines reflected transition through structure rather than through visible completion. Adv. PL PU5.5 E1 showed clear bent descent-path emergence beyond tuck criteria, with early adv-like linemaintenance for roughly 1–2 reps before later reps gradually shifted toward a more vertical / tuck-L-sit-like angle. The late-rep limiter was insufficient protraction output rather than shoulder blockage.BAPL45 5.5 E2 remained volumetrically performable despite shoulder load/signals, and the final limiterwas cumulative output / concentration loss rather than structural failure. This means the push-complexlines were not blocked; they were transitional and still reorganizing under cost.
Secondary lines
Str FL Row / Adv. 360 Pull
These lines showed that pull-side transition was also becoming more real rather than merelyexploratory. Str FL Row 3.5 E2 confirmed actual row emergence beyond simple hold survival. Adv. 360Pull 5.5 E2 repeated stably even under residual DOMS / heavy-body condition, with BL recovery burdenlower than before and adv lever fixation feeling more natural than in the earlier 3-level phase.
Conditioning line (separate from stage-transition evaluation)
Pistol 7.7 should remain outside the main stage-transition interpretation. It functioned as aconditioning-fixed line throughout the month. Under 1:30 rest and relatively fast tempo, the free-legpattern remained stable and even became more settled in later sets. Burpee progressed from stableeven-paced output into a clear 4′08″ PB by 3/29. Conditioning therefore served as a stable parallel linerather than a transition indicator.
Signal / fatigue status
March included a real downshift window, but the important point is that the downshift did notcollapse the month. After the interruption, runtime continuity returned. Shoulder signals appearedmostly as local, task-bound load signals rather than persistent structural warnings. By month end, thesystem was again capable of producing clean session closures with manageable residual cost.
Conclusion
March was a 3-level stage-transition month with interruption inside it. It should not be framed as afresh 7-level expansion month. The real story was that stage transition had already begun around lateFebruary to early March, then passed through a neural downshift / break period, yet still finished themonth with visible reconnection and clearer runtime continuity. HSPU moved out of purefragmentation, A.OAP asymmetry narrowed, complex push / pull lines became more structurallyreadable, and conditioning remained stable as a separate fixed line. With 23 total sessions, March wasnot low-volume. It was a disrupted but still substantial month that ended in reconnected transitionrather than regression.

NSS-77TR RECORD
⸻
NSS-77TR — Monthly Core Summary [2026-01]

January functioned as a STABILIZATION → LEVEL TRANSITION phase, not a recovery month and not a peak-chasing month.

Total sessions reached 26. The longest continuous run was 14 consecutive sessions. There were no fixed rest days. Reset logic remained external-event–triggered only.

All sessions strictly followed Signal > Plan, with no forced progression.

Primary progression lines

Level 6 → Level 7 transition

L Pull-up progressed from 6.6 into 7.7 E1, which was successfully entered and completed.

WHSPU progressed from 6.6 into 7.7 E1, with controlled ROM modulation.

No grinding, forced reps, or structural compromise appeared during the level transition.

Advanced FL Row

Advanced FL Row 6.6 stabilized through E2.

ROM was auto-gated by volume. Trajectory consistency improved, and the most stable execution was observed on 1/31.

Systemic cost reached its lowest level to date.

BAPL

BAPL progressed into 6.6.

The line behaved as an emergence-based skill rather than an output-limited task. Trunk-led rotation proved superior to limb-driven attempts.

Shoulder signals appeared only with alignment loss, and no pain signals were recorded.

Conditioning

Burpee 40×3 progressed from paced completion to a new PB of 5′24″ total.

The PB was achieved during a low-intent session, indicating elastic efficiency gain. Conditioning cost remained low relative to output.

Assisted Pistol

Assisted Pistol identified the ROM gate as neural / structural rather than strength-based.

The arms-forward + core-lead strategy released the depth restriction, and balance asymmetry reduced across sessions.

System behavior & signals

Shoulders

No pain signals appeared throughout the month.

Residual echoes were transient and self-resolving. End-of-month shoulder condition was the best since mid-December.

Lumbar / core

Occasional myofascial pop events appeared during HLR.

These were interpreted as axial fatigue markers. Immediate self-termination was applied correctly, with no carryover or instability.

DOMS / pump

DOMS remained minimal to absent despite increased volume.

Pump was transient. Shape re-stabilized rapidly after sessions.

Adaptation favored internal density and coordination rather than visible swelling or fatigue residue.

Structural & neural adaptation

The concept of fixed rest effectively dissolved.

Recovery was managed through output modulation rather than time-off.

The 7-rep zones were perceived as neural capacity tests. High-frequency execution improved next-day performance, and movement control became increasingly automatic.

Key characteristics of January

Output became quieter, not louder.

Failures were replaced by early modulation or clean termination.

Logs shifted from sensation-heavy to structure-heavy.

Stability allowed Level 7 entry without a preparatory deload.

Conclusion

January confirmed that the NSS-77TR system can sustain high frequency, Level 7 workloads, and no fixed rest days without loss of structural integrity or signal clarity.

The month marks a transition from capacity building to emergent skill expansion under stable load.

System state at month end: locked, quiet, and expandable.

Next phase

New movement entries at lower levels, especially Lv-up 3.x, can proceed safely.

The Level 7 base remains intact and non-fragile.
